sections.h2: How can a Troy homeowner sell without months of showings?
sections.html:
Fast options in Troy are an as-is cash purchase or a listing priced to sell, and the right pick follows the house itself. A downtown address inside the Historic District raises different questions than a recent subdivision home, so decide where your property stands first.

  • Agent listing: reaches Dayton-area buyers, with an inspection and loan approval still ahead of closing.
  • Owner-handled sale: you draft the contract, deliver the disclosure form and line up the deed.
  • Direct as-is purchase: the buyer inherits the repairs, and you can set closing to fit your move.

Any route ends the same way: the deed clears the Miami County Engineer and Auditor, then goes to the Recorder.

sections.h2: What is Troy, Ohio like for a seller?
sections.html:
Troy seats Miami County and is its largest city, set on the Great Miami River roughly 19 miles north of Dayton. Surveyors platted it around 1807, and the post office dates to 1824. Troy was among the cities touched by the Great Flood of 1913. The city measures 11.94 square miles, with 11.72 of land.

The older core is distinctive. Overfield Tavern, from 1808, is now a museum, and the Troy-Hayner Cultural Center fills a 1914 Romanesque mansion. The Hobart Welded Steel House Company built just 22 prefabricated steel houses, every one in Troy, and 16 survive on the National Register of Historic Places. The Hobart Institute of Welding Technology opened in 1930, and the Troy Public Square and Miami County Courthouse are also listed.

Troy's Historic District is an overlay running roughly from the Miami River on the north to Canal Street on the south, and from Oxford Street on the west to Clay Street on the east. That footprint matches the city's edge when it became county seat in 1807. The Planning Commission reviews alterations there, so check before you repaint, reside or replace windows for a sale.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers show for Troy?
sections.html:
Troy is growing. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 27,344 residents, up 3.8 percent from the April 2020 base, and each census from 1990 to 2020 counted more people than the one before.

sections.h2: Which Troy schools do buyers look at?
sections.html:
Most of Troy belongs to Troy City Schools: the high school covers grades 9 to 12, the junior high grades 7 and 8, and the elementary buildings are Concord, Cookson, Forest, Heywood, Hook, Kyle and Van Cleve. A slice of the city falls in the Miami East Local School District, so verify the district for your exact address before you advertise it.

Private options include Troy Christian (Pre-K to 12), St. Patrick School for kindergarten to 8 and Miami Montessori School. The Troy-Miami County Public Library has three locations in the city.

sections.h2: How do Troy's property maintenance and zoning rules affect a sale?
sections.html:
The city enforces the International Property Maintenance Code on existing homes and other structures, and ignoring it can bring penalties from the courts. Property maintenance staff log complaints and also find problems themselves. Troy publishes an exterior checklist, and walking your property with it before you list is an easy way to catch peeling paint, broken steps or overgrown yards.

If you added a shed, deck, garage or pool, ask the city's Planning and Zoning Division whether the zoning permit was finished, because a buyer's inspector or lender may ask for the paper trail.

sections.h2: What does Troy require about water service lines and utilities?
sections.html:
Troy houses built before February 1, 1944 could have lead water service lines, since the city banned lead in 1944. Because of the EPA's Lead and Copper Rule, the city is inventorying service line materials and mails owners of those homes a yearly letter until the line is replaced or its material is verified. A city technician can inspect in about 15 minutes on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. (937-335-4151), or you can self-report online.

On the buyer's side, the Utility Billing office at City Hall, 100 S. Market Street, opens an owner's service with photo ID plus a deed, closing papers or an accepted purchase contract. It also requires that any delinquency be resolved first, so settle your own account and call the office about the handover.

sections.h2: How does a Troy deed move through Miami County?
sections.html:
The standards Miami County adopted on August 12, 2025 set the sequence. The Engineer's office approves the instrument first. The Auditor then takes a completed DTE 100 statement of value or a DTE 100 EX exemption form, and the Recorder will file a deed only after it bears both approval stamps.

  • Seller names on the deed must match the previous deed, or an affidavit under Ohio Revised Code 5301.252 has to explain the gap in title.
  • A land contract needs Engineer approval and an Auditor date stamp before it is recorded.
  • Fee checks go to the Miami County Auditor for the exact amount, because overpayments are refused.
  • The Auditor's website offers a conveyance fee calculator that adds in the parcel transfer fee.

Ohio Revised Code 322.02 puts the county transfer tax on the grantor. The same standards cover next-of-kin affidavits, survivorship transfers and transfer on death affidavits, which matters when a Troy house comes from an estate.

sections.h2: When does a direct sale suit a Troy house?
sections.html:
It tends to fit three kinds of Troy property. The first is a pre-1944 house with an unverified water line and old systems. The second is a rental, since about 34.5 percent of occupied Troy homes are not owner-occupied. The third is an estate house where heirs live elsewhere.

In each case, ask the buyer in writing who handles the lead line inventory, any open permit and the county transfer paperwork, and keep a copy of the signed purchase contract for the utility office.

sections.h2: What does the Ohio disclosure statute say about timing?
sections.html:
Under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30, a buyer who first sees the property disclosure form after signing may rescind in writing within three business days of receipt. That right ends 30 days after acceptance or at closing, whichever is earlier. A buyer who received the form before making an offer has no rescission right.

So hand over the form with the first showing packet. A seller who inherited the house and did not live in it during the prior year is exempt.

faqs.q: Where do I file a deed for a Troy house?
faqs.a: Miami County handles it. The Engineer approves the description, the Auditor processes the conveyance form, and the Recorder files the deed. Begin with the Engineer.

faqs.q: Does Troy have a historic district that limits changes?
faqs.a: Inside the overlay, yes: the Planning Commission reviews alterations. The district is generally bounded by the Miami River, Clay, Canal and Oxford streets, and Planning and Zoning can tell you if your address is in it.

faqs.q: Will an old Troy home need a lead service line inspection?
faqs.a: Only homes built before February 1, 1944 are in the inventory. Those owners receive a yearly letter until the line is replaced or its material is confirmed by inspection or self-report.

faqs.q: Who pays the conveyance fee when a Troy house sells?
faqs.a: You do, as grantor, under Ohio Revised Code 322.02. Run your sale price through the Miami County Auditor's online calculator, which includes the parcel transfer fee, before the closing date.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Troy house with unpermitted work?
faqs.a: Yes, though a buyer's inspector may ask about permits. Check with Planning and Zoning on any shed, deck or pool, and document or correct it before you list.
